Consistency.justification: The proposal is strongly aligned with the supplied idea. It retains the central retina-inspired concepts of dynamic gazing, coherent FMCW LiDAR, an agile external-cavity laser, reconfigurable electro-optic frequency combs, parallel sensing channels, and cooperative camera-LiDAR sensing. Its learned controller is a coherent extension of the original hardware-focused idea, and the experiments directly test adaptive allocation under power, bandwidth, and latency constraints. The proposal also identifies relevant adjacent work in adaptive coherent LiDAR, foveated sensing, and learned control. The main limitation is that the relationship between individual comb-tone controls and spatial or angular beam allocation is asserted rather than fully specified; thus, some proposed actions may depend on additional beam-steering or channel-routing hardware not explicitly included in the core idea.

Clarity.justification: The motivation, hypothesis, controller inputs and outputs, experimental sequence, baselines, metrics, ablations, and major risks are presented in a logical and understandable manner. The separation into simulator development, policy training, simulation evaluation, ablation studies, and hardware-in-loop validation provides a clear research workflow. However, several important details remain ambiguous: how comb lines map to spatial angles, how per-tone phase affects the sensing objective, how mutual information or posterior entropy will be estimated, what scene representation and detector will be used, and what latency, power, and reconfiguration limits define hardware feasibility. The proposal also predicts significant improvements without defining quantitative success thresholds.

Novelty.justification: The most original aspect is the hardware-aware learning of discrete-continuous photonic sensing actions, including tone selection, amplitude allocation, dwell scheduling, and chirp adaptation, using camera observations and LiDAR history. Combining differentiable photonic simulation, information efficiency objectives, saccadic scheduling, and hardware-in-loop deployment is a notable and potentially valuable synthesis. Nevertheless, the underlying retina-inspired adaptive LiDAR architecture, dynamic zooming, camera-guided sensing, active perception, and learned sensor scheduling all have substantial precedent. Given the cited 2024 integrated adaptive coherent LiDAR demonstration, the proposal is primarily a learned control and co-design extension rather than a fundamentally new sensing architecture. The novelty claim would be stronger with a more systematic comparison against prior learned active LiDAR, adaptive waveform design, and neural sensor-scheduling literature.

Soundness.justification: The proposal uses sensible foundations: coherent FMCW modeling, differentiable simulation, recurrent multimodal policies, constrained optimization, reinforcement learning, calibration studies, domain randomization, and hardware-in-loop evaluation. The planned baselines, ablations, robustness tests, and sim-to-real measurements are appropriate. However, the methodology is not yet rigorous enough to establish that the full action space is physically identifiable and controllable. A clear forward model connecting tone frequency, amplitude, phase, chirp parameters, angular allocation, optical power, beat-frequency bandwidth, and velocity-range ambiguity is missing. Mutual information per photon is difficult to estimate reliably in high-dimensional scenes, but no estimator or approximation is specified. PPO may also be sample-inefficient for the proposed hybrid action space. Speckle, coherent interference, detector saturation, laser phase noise, comb-line crosstalk, calibration drift, and safety constraints are mentioned only partially or at a high level. Finally, comparing against the published 2024 strategy only 'if available' weakens the evaluation plan.

Feasibility.justification: Most individual components are implementable with current technology: physics-based simulation, compact multimodal policies, constrained scheduling, FPGA or real-time-PC inference, and tabletop FMCW experiments. The staged plan and fallback options improve practicality. At the same time, jointly optimizing discrete tone selection, continuous amplitudes, phases, dwell times, chirps, and spatial allocation is a large and difficult control problem. Independent high-speed per-tone amplitude and phase control may require programmable filtering or modulation hardware that is not standard on many electro-optic comb platforms. Millisecond closed-loop latency, synchronized reconfiguration, calibration, eye-safe peak-power control, and sim-to-real transfer create substantial engineering risk. The proposed testbed emulates selectable comb tones rather than necessarily demonstrating the claimed fully integrated chip-scale system, so successful hardware-in-loop results would not by themselves establish end-to-end chip-scale feasibility.

Significance.justification: Efficient allocation of optical power, temporal bandwidth, angular resolution, and computation is an important problem for practical 4D sensing. If the method improves detection and depth or velocity estimation under fixed energy and latency budgets, it could contribute meaningfully to robotics, autonomous systems, and photonic sensor design. Open-source simulation and interface tools could also benefit the community. The potential impact is somewhat moderated by the dependence on specialized coherent LiDAR hardware, uncertain transfer from tabletop demonstrations to outdoor operation, and the possibility that simpler camera-guided heuristics capture much of the attainable gain. Demonstrating robust improvements under realistic weather, reflectance, interference, and safety conditions would be needed to support transformative impact.

strengths: Strong alignment with the retina-inspired adaptive 4D LiDAR idea and a well-structured progression from simulation through ablation to hardware-in-loop testing.
Promising integration of learned active sensing, information and task-aware objectives, hardware constraints, multimodal feedback, and photonic control.
Appropriate attention to baselines, robustness, latency, energy use, sim-to-real transfer, and reproducible open-source outputs.
weaknesses: The physical mapping from comb-tone and chirp controls to angular sensing allocation and measurable information gain is insufficiently specified.
The novelty is partly incremental relative to existing adaptive coherent LiDAR, foveated sensing, waveform optimization, and learned active-perception methods.
The proposed hybrid optimization and mutual-information objectives lack enough algorithmic detail to assess stability, sample efficiency, or statistical validity.
The hardware-in-loop system may only emulate key controls and therefore may not substantiate the stronger claim of real-time deployment on a fully integrated chip-scale platform.
